title: Religion and Morality in Western Philosophy

summaries.example: Imagine a class deciding whether it is fair to leave someone out of a game. One student might say, “We should include them because everyone deserves kindness.” Another might say, “Our religion teaches us to care for neighbors.” Philosophers ask whether these are two different reasons or two parts of one moral life.
summaries.summary: This entry follows the long history of ideas about religion and morality in Western philosophy. Morality means the customs and habits that shape ideas about how people should live. Religion is harder to define because religions have different beliefs and practices. In ancient Greece, Plato and Aristotle connected the best human life with becoming wise, just, and more like the divine. Other Greek schools, such as Epicureanism and Stoicism, also linked human happiness with ideas about the gods, although they understood the gods differently. In the Hebrew Bible and the New Testament, God’s commands, promises, love, and care for the weak are central. Jesus is presented as teaching love of God, love of neighbor, and even love of enemies. Medieval Jewish, Christian, and Muslim thinkers brought these traditions into conversation with Greek philosophy. Later philosophers asked whether morality comes from God’s will, human reason, feelings, nature, social agreement, or human choice. Contemporary thinkers continue to debate religious commands, virtues, natural law, justice, human rights, and whether religious reasons belong in public discussion. The history shows that religion and morality have often been closely connected, even though many people today separate them.
key_ideas: For much of Western history, people connected religion with questions about right and wrong.
Ancient Greek thinkers often said that people should become more like the divine by developing wisdom and virtue.
The Hebrew Bible and the New Testament often present morality through God’s commands, love, covenant, and care for others.
Later thinkers disagreed about whether morality needs religion, reason, feelings, nature, society, or some combination.
Some modern philosophers defended religious morality, while others tried to explain ethics without religious belief.
summaries.why_it_matters: People make important choices about fairness, kindness, responsibility, and justice. This history helps us understand why people give different reasons for those choices. It also shows that religious and nonreligious thinkers have sometimes agreed about moral goals while disagreeing about their foundation. Learning how to compare these reasons can help us listen carefully and discuss difficult questions respectfully.

important_terms.definition: Ideas and habits that help people think about how they should live and what makes a life good.
A system of beliefs and practices connected with a special relationship to gods or other divine beings. Religions can be very different from one another.
A rule or instruction believed to come from God or another authority.
A good quality of character, such as courage, fairness, or self-control.
The question of whether something is right because God commands it, or whether God commands it because it is already right.

questions_to_think_about: Can people who follow different religions agree about some moral rules?
Is an action good because a divine being commands it, or would it be good even without that command?
Can someone be a good person without belonging to a religion?
Why might people want their moral reasons to be understood by others?

summaries.example: Suppose a city is deciding whether to adopt a law protecting a vulnerable minority. A religious citizen might appeal to divine commands about loving one’s neighbor or the equal worth of human beings. Another citizen might appeal to Kantian respect for persons, Rawls’s concern for fairness, or a secular account of human rights. The dispute is not only about the policy; it is also about which reasons can justify a law to people who do not share the same comprehensive view of life.
summaries.summary: The entry traces how Western philosophers have understood the relationship between morality and religion from Homer and the Presocratics through contemporary ethics. It begins by warning that both terms are contested. Morality concerns customs and standards for living well, while religion is best treated as a group of related belief-practice systems rather than something with one defining essence. Greek philosophy often portrays the divine as drawing human beings toward wisdom, justice, virtue, and flourishing. Plato’s discussion of holiness raises the Euthyphro question, while Aristotle’s virtue ethics places human excellence and contemplation in a theological setting. Epicureans and Stoics offer different accounts of divine involvement and human freedom from anxiety. In the Hebrew Bible and New Testament, command, covenant, love, sin, forgiveness, and the care of neighbors are central. Medieval thinkers such as Augustine, Maimonides, Muslim theologians, Abelard, Aquinas, and Scotus develop competing accounts of reason, revelation, will, freedom, natural law, intention, and happiness. Modern philosophers increasingly examine morality through rationalism, empiricism, sentiment, autonomy, social order, and historical development. Kant connects moral obligation with freedom and practical reason, while Hume and later thinkers argue that moral life may be grounded in sentiment or social practice rather than theology. In the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, existentialists, analytic philosophers, Rawls, Habermas, virtue theorists, natural-law theorists, and defenders of divine command continue the debate. The entry’s historical conclusion is not that one side has won, but that religious and moral reflection remain deeply connected even when many ethical theories proceed
key_ideas: The entry presents a chronology in which Greek philosophical accounts and Jewish-Christian accounts begin differently but repeatedly influence one another.
A major contrast is between morality as attraction toward the good or the divine and morality as obedience to divine command; the contrast is not absolute.
The Euthyphro problem asks whether holiness or goodness depends on divine approval, or whether divine approval responds to an independent standard.
Medieval thinkers developed different syntheses of revelation, reason, virtue, natural law, freedom, and human happiness. Muslim, Jewish, and Christian thinkers also disagreed among themselves.
Modern philosophy increasingly explored reason, experience, sentiment, autonomy, social agreement, and historical power as sources or explanations of morality.

Contemporary debates include divine command theory, virtue ethics, natural law, human rights, public reason, religious participation in public life, and the possibility of moral reasoning across religious differences.
summaries.why_it_matters: Moral disagreements often involve different ideas about human nature, happiness, authority, freedom, and what counts as a good reason. Religion can support moral commitments, but it can also be criticized or interpreted in competing ways. Nonreligious theories face their own questions about obligation, motivation, and justification. Studying this history makes it easier to distinguish a moral conclusion from the deeper argument offered for it, and to recognize that public ethical discussion may involve both shared values and profound disagreement.

important_terms.definition: The customs, habits, and standards that shape judgments about how people ought to live; the entry treats it as broadly interchangeable with ethics.
A family of belief-and-practice systems involving a binding relationship to divine or spiritual beings; the entry stresses that no single essence fits every religion.
The view that moral obligation is grounded in divine will or command, though philosophers disagree about whether this makes morality arbitrary.
An account of morality emphasizing excellent character and the activities that constitute human flourishing, especially in Aristotle and later virtue ethics.
A theory that human beings participate through practical reason in an order directed toward the good; Aquinas connects natural law with virtues and friendship with God.
Kant’s principle that one should act only on reasons one could will as universal laws and must treat humanity as an end, never merely as a tool.
A proposed basis for moral claims that does not depend on religious revelation or divine authority; philosophers disagree about whether such a basis can be adequate.

questions_to_think_about: Does grounding obligation in divine command solve the problem of moral authority, or does it create a problem of arbitrariness?
Can a moral theory respect people as ends while also aiming at the greatest total happiness?
Should citizens use explicitly religious reasons when arguing about public laws? What would fairness require?
How do virtue ethics and rule-centered theories describe moral education differently?
Can religious and nonreligious traditions share moral conclusions without sharing the same ultimate justification?

summaries.example: A student notices that a new classmate is being ignored. One friend says, “We should include them because people have a duty to care for others.” Another says, “We should include them because kindness helps everyone flourish.” A third says, “My faith teaches love of neighbor.” Philosophy asks whether these reasons conflict, whether one is stronger, and whether people need the same beliefs in order to agree on what to do.
summaries.summary: This entry explores a very old question: how are religion and morality connected? Morality means the standards and habits people use when thinking about how to live. Religion is more difficult to define because religions have many different beliefs and practices. The entry follows the topic through five periods. Ancient Greek thinkers often connected the best life with virtue, reason, justice, and becoming more like the divine. Plato’s conversation with Euthyphro raises a famous problem: is something holy because the gods love it, or do the gods love it because it is holy? Aristotle also connects human flourishing with virtue and contemplation of what is divine. Epicureans and Stoics disagree about the gods but still connect the best life with religious ideas. In the Hebrew Bible and New Testament, morality is strongly connected with God’s commands, covenant, love, forgiveness, and responsibility toward neighbors and enemies. Medieval Jewish, Christian, and Muslim philosophers debated whether reason can know right and wrong, whether God’s will creates moral standards, and how much freedom people have. Thinkers such as Augustine and Aquinas joined Greek philosophy with Christianity, while others emphasized will, intention, or divine sovereignty. In modern philosophy, ethics became more independent from theology for some thinkers. Hume emphasized moral feeling, Kant emphasized rational duty, and utilitarian thinkers emphasized happiness and consequences. Contemporary philosophers disagree about whether public morality should rely on religious reasons, whether human rights need a religious foundation, and whether virtues or divine commands best explain moral life. The entry shows a long conversation rather than one simple answer.
key_ideas: Greek philosophers and Jewish and Christian scriptures connect moral life with religion, but they do so in different ways.
Plato and Aristotle often describe goodness as something that draws people toward a better way of living, while biblical traditions emphasize God’s commands and covenant.
These differences are not complete opposites: Greek thinkers discuss duties and disciplined desire, while biblical traditions also emphasize love, blessing, and human flourishing.
Medieval philosophers combined Greek philosophy with Jewish, Christian, and Muslim ideas, producing disagreements about reason, revelation, freedom, intention, and God’s will.
Modern philosophers gave more attention to reason, experience, feelings, society, personal freedom, and whether ethics can stand without theology.
Contemporary philosophers continue debating justice, rights, virtue, public reasoning, and the role of religious commitments in shared political life.
summaries.why_it_matters: Questions about religion and morality affect everyday behavior and public decisions. People may agree that justice or compassion matters but disagree about why. Understanding the main arguments helps us avoid assuming that all religious thinkers agree or that all nonreligious thinkers reject moral rules. It also gives us tools for discussing serious disagreements without treating other people unfairly.

important_terms.definition: A set of customs and standards that guides ideas about how people should live and what counts as a good life.
A group of beliefs and practices involving a binding relationship with gods or spiritual beings; the entry says religions share similarities without having one exact definition.
An instruction that tells someone what to do, especially one understood as coming from God or another authority.
A stable good trait, such as courage, fairness, wisdom, or self-control, that helps a person live well.
A theory that judges morality partly by the quality of a person’s character and by whether actions express good traits.
The problem of deciding whether something is right because the gods approve it, or whether the gods approve it because it is already right.
The idea that human reason can discover or participate in standards directing people toward the good; Aquinas links it with divine wisdom.

questions_to_think_about: Can two people agree that an action is wrong while giving completely different reasons?
Does a command become morally good simply because a powerful being gives it?
Why might a philosopher think that good character matters more than following rules?
Should religious beliefs be included in arguments about laws that affect everyone?
What might be gained or lost when morality is explained without religion?
